delete an inline-table-valued key
delete key inside a packed inline table (regression)
cases.note: Regression: an inline table's entries are comma-separated on one physical line, not one-per-line like a block table, so `deleteKey`'s generic line-based delete (built for the block shape) used to delete the whole containing line — here, the entire (single-line) document — leaving an empty file that TOML's empty-document-is-an-empty-table grammar then accepted, silently committing the data loss instead of erroring. Deleting a key *inside* a packed inline table must only remove that key.

cases.id: delete first key of a packed inline table
delete only key of a single-entry inline table (regression)
cases.note: Regression: deleting the *only* key of a single-entry inline table must leave an empty inline table `{}`, not delete the braces with the line. The old block-shaped line delete wiped the whole `point = { x = 1 }` line, which TOML's empty-document-is-an-empty-table grammar then silently accepted, committing the data loss to disk instead of preserving `point = {}`.

cases.id: delete last key of a multi-line inline table (regression)
cases.note: Regression: deleting the *last* key of a one-entry-per-line inline table used to strand the predecessor's separator comma before the closing brace — which TOML forbids (no trailing comma in an inline table). The flow-aware splice drops the preceding comma instead.

delete the only AoT element leaves an empty array in the parent's body [1]
cases.note: The only element of an array of tables leaves the array, emptied, as the last item of an inline array does: `x = []`, written in the body of the table that holds `x` — the root's entries above the first header, `[t]`'s under its header, an element's under its `[[a]]` — where an entry inserted into that table goes. A table with no header of its own (`t` made by `[[t.x]]` alone, or by a dotted line) has no body, so the key path from the nearest table that has one is written as a dotted key there. The comment block above `[[x]]` and the comment ending its line stay, around `x = []`. The Zig test also reads the array back as an empty sequence, which `= []` pins.

cases.id: deleteContainer of a header table takes a multi-line dotted child whole
cases.note: `x` is a dotted table under `[a]` spread over two lines; the second line is in no node span of `x`'s keyvalue, and a gather that took the entry's own line would have left `x.z = 2` behind to become a root key.

cases.id: moveContainer to before a root dotted table is refused, not a reparented table
cases.note: Zig error EditReadsBackWrong. A dotted-only table has no `[` line, which the old header-line sniff refused as a destination; it is a section node like any other. But `[b]` set down above the root's `d.k = 0` takes that line into `b`, where `d` reads back as `b.d`: the move guard refuses.

cases.id: edits after a refused one and a missing one read the source as it stands
cases.note: Zig errors EditReadsBackWrong, NotFound. The guards compare with the parse the editor already held, kept from the reparse that would have freed it, and hand its buffer back when nothing was spliced: an edit after a refused one, and after one that found nothing to delete, reads the source as it stands.

cases.id: non-YAML formats keep vivifying through flow seeds
cases.note: The empty seed is YAML-specific: `a =` is not a TOML value, and the flow chain is the idiomatic intermediate form for the dotted-key formats. The Zig test reads its TOML source as TOML 1.0; the binding's `toml` dialect is 1.1, and the seed is the same in both.
